To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
patients with angina with normal coronary arteries and patients with acute myocardial infarcation with normal coronary arteries show evidence of endothelial dysfunction.
patients with syndrome X have an impaired coronary flow reserve and abnormal endothelium-dependent vasodilation.
endothelial dysfunction plays a key role in patients with anginal chest pain and normal coronary arteries.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the vascular endothelial in patients with anginal symptoms with normal coronary arteries.
the role of the vascular endothelial in patients with anginal pain or acute myocardial ischemia with normal coronary arteries.
the evaluation of endothelial dysfunction in patients with anginal pain and normal coronary angiograms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the syndrome of angina pectororis with normal coronary angiography and the acute myocardial infraction with angiographically normal arteries are still unclear.
endothelial dysfunction is the most probable explanation for the syndrome of chest pain with normal coronary arteries.
endothelial dysfunction is an important mechanism in patients with anginal chest pain and normal coronary arteries.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the vascular endothelum is an important target in the pathogenesis of both stable angina and acute myocardial infraction with normal coronary arteries.
endothelial dysfunction may be the common denominator in the pathophysiology of these syndromes.
the syndrome of chest pain with normal coronary arteries is a heterogeneous disorder with a multifactorial pathophysiology.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the endothelium is a major determinant of coronary vascular resistance and that the presence of endothelial dysfunction in patients with syndrome-X and in patients with an acute MI and angiographically normal arteries may be the underlying pathophysiological mechanism responsible for these syndromes.
